source: MBAX 6215 Midterm Study Guide F26 + cheat sheet

cards.prompt: Formula, meaning, and a worked example
cards.back_html:
Sharpe = (Rp − Rf) ÷ σp

Excess return earned per unit of total risk (standard deviation). Higher is better.

Example: Rp 10%, Rf 3%, σ 14% → 7 ÷ 14 = 0.50

  • Use it when the portfolio is the client's whole portfolio, so total risk (including diversifiable risk) matters.
  • Penalizes upside and downside volatility equally.
  • Comparing funds: the higher Sharpe delivered more return per unit of risk taken.

cards.prompt: Formula, meaning, and a worked example
cards.back_html:
Sortino = (Rp − Rf or MAR) ÷ downside deviation

Excess return per unit of downside risk. Only volatility below the target (Rf or a minimum acceptable return, MAR) counts, so upside swings are not penalized.

Example: Rp 10%, Rf 3%, downside deviation 8% → 7 ÷ 8 = 0.875

  • Use it for asymmetric return patterns (options strategies, hedge funds) or loss-focused clients.
  • Same numerator as Sharpe; only the denominator differs.

cards.prompt: Formula, meaning, and a worked example
cards.back_html:
Treynor = (Rp − Rf) ÷ βp

Excess return per unit of systematic (market) risk.

Example: Rp 10%, Rf 3%, β 1.2 → 7% ÷ 1.2 = 5.83%

  • Use it when the fund is one piece of a well-diversified portfolio, so unsystematic risk washes out and only beta matters.
  • A fund can win on Treynor but lose on Sharpe if it carries a lot of unsystematic risk (high σ, low β).

cards.front: After-tax return on bonds (and tax-equivalent yield)
cards.prompt: Formula, meaning, and a worked example
cards.back_html:
After-tax yield = taxable yield × (1 − t)
Tax-equivalent yield (TEY) = muni yield ÷ (1 − t)

t = the investor's marginal tax rate (the rate on the next dollar).

Example: 32% bracket. Corporate 5.0% → 5.0 × 0.68 = 3.40% after tax. Muni 3.5% → TEY 3.5 ÷ 0.68 = 5.15%. The muni wins either way.

  • Corporate: taxed federal + state. Treasury: federal only (state-exempt). In-state muni: usually exempt from both.
  • With state tax, use a combined rate (simple version: federal + state).
  • Break-even bracket = 1 − (muni ÷ taxable). 1 − 3.5/5.0 = 30%; above it, the muni wins.

cards.prompt: Formula, meaning, and a worked example
cards.back_html:
Average cost per share = total dollars invested ÷ total shares bought

Invest a fixed dollar amount at regular intervals regardless of price, so you buy more shares when prices are low.

Example: $300/month at $10, $15, $6 → 30 + 20 + 50 = 100 shares for $900. Average cost $9.00 vs average price $10.33.

  • Average cost is always ≤ the average price (it is a harmonic mean).
  • Average price = simple average of the prices paid; don't confuse the two on the exam.

cards.prompt: Formula, meaning, and a worked example
cards.back_html:
Real return = (1 + nominal) ÷ (1 + inflation) − 1

The growth in purchasing power after inflation (the Fisher relation).

Example: nominal 8%, inflation 3% → 1.08 ÷ 1.03 − 1 = 4.85%

  • Shortcut nominal − inflation (5%) slightly overstates it; use the exact formula on the exam.
  • A 2% return with 3% inflation is a negative real return (−0.97%).

cards.prompt: Define it, give an example, and explain why it matters
cards.back_html:
Kahneman & Tversky (1979): people judge outcomes as gains or losses relative to a reference point, not by final wealth.

  • Loss aversion: losses hurt about 2× as much as equal gains feel good.
  • Diminishing sensitivity: risk-averse with gains (take the sure $500), risk-seeking with losses (gamble to avoid a sure $500 loss). Value curve: concave for gains, convex and steeper for losses.
  • Probability weighting: overweight small probabilities (lotteries, insurance).

Investing impact: the disposition effect: selling winners too early and holding losers too long.

Fix: judge results at the whole-portfolio level; pre-set, rules-based selling.

cards.prompt: Define it, give an example, and explain why it matters
cards.back_html:
Barry Schwartz: more options lead to decision paralysis, worse choices, and less satisfaction with the choice made.

Example: 401(k) participation falls as the number of fund options rises; an employee faced with 40 funds never enrolls.

Damage: inaction, cash drag, naive diversification (spreading 1/n across whatever is listed).

Fix: curated short menus, good defaults (auto-enrollment, target-date funds), adviser narrows to 2–3 choices.

cards.prompt: Define it, give an example, and explain why it matters
cards.back_html:
The mental discomfort of holding conflicting beliefs, or of seeing evidence that a past decision was wrong. People ease it by ignoring or rationalizing the evidence.

Example: a stock you picked falls on bad news, and you decide "the market just doesn't get it" instead of re-examining the thesis.

Damage: holding losers, selective attention to information; feeds confirmation bias.

Fix: written investment thesis with sell triggers; outside review of positions.

cards.prompt: Define it, give an example, the damage it does, and how to overcome it
cards.back_html:
Clinging to a prior view and under-reacting to new information; updating too slowly. Cognitive

Example: an analyst barely revises a forecast after a huge earnings miss.

Damage: slow reaction to real changes; holding stale positions.

Fix: deliberately weigh new data; ask "what would change my mind?" and act when it happens.

Don't confuse: confirmation bias filters information; conservatism under-weights it.

cards.prompt: Define it, give an example, the damage it does, and how to overcome it
cards.back_html:
Seeking out and favoring information that supports existing beliefs while discounting contrary evidence. Cognitive

Example: reading only bullish forums about a favorite stock.

Damage: concentration, overconfidence, ignoring warning signs.

Fix: actively seek the bear case; assign a devil's advocate; use objective criteria.

Don't confuse: it is a cause of overconfidence, and differs from conservatism (which is slow updating).

cards.prompt: Define it, give an example, the damage it does, and how to overcome it
cards.back_html:
Judging by stereotype or resemblance to a familiar pattern, ignoring base rates and sample size. Cognitive

Examples: "great company = great stock" (ignoring price); chasing last year's top fund; assuming a few good years prove skill.

Damage: overpaying for quality, performance chasing.

Fix: check base rates and valuation; demand long track records.

Don't confuse: recency overweights what just happened; representativeness matches patterns or stereotypes.

cards.prompt: Define it, give an example, the damage it does, and how to overcome it
cards.back_html:
Treating money differently depending on the mental "bucket" it sits in, instead of as one fungible pool. Cognitive

Examples: paying 22% on a credit card while holding a 1% "vacation fund"; gambling dividends or "house money" while being careful with salary.

Damage: ignores correlations and opportunity cost; inefficient overall portfolio.

Fix: look at total net worth and the total portfolio; goal-based buckets are fine if the whole is managed together.

cards.prompt: Define it, give an example, the damage it does, and how to overcome it
cards.back_html:
Fixating on an initial number (purchase price, past high, first estimate) and adjusting too little from it. Cognitive

Example: refusing to sell until the stock "gets back to what I paid."

Damage: holding losers, unrealistic price targets.

Fix: ask "would I buy this today at today's price?"; base decisions on current fundamentals.

Don't confuse: anchoring sticks to a number; framing reacts to how a choice is worded.

cards.prompt: Define it, give an example, the damage it does, and how to overcome it
cards.back_html:
Making different decisions from the same facts depending on how they are presented (gain vs loss, % vs $). Cognitive

Example: preferring "a 90% chance of beating cash" over "a 10% chance of losing to cash."

Damage: inconsistent risk choices; risk questionnaires give different answers depending on wording.

Fix: restate the choice several ways; focus on outcomes and probabilities, not the wording.

cards.prompt: Define it, give an example, the damage it does, and how to overcome it
cards.back_html:
Overweighting recent events and extrapolating them forward, while discounting long-run history. Cognitive

Example: expecting 20% returns after two strong years; panic selling after a crash because "it will keep falling."

Damage: buy high, sell low; performance chasing.

Fix: long-run return data; written rebalancing rules; an IPS that sets the allocation in advance.

cards.prompt: Define it, give an example, the damage it does, and how to overcome it
cards.back_html:
Losses feel roughly twice as painful as equal gains feel good, so people work too hard to avoid losses. Emotional

Examples: holding losers to avoid "realizing" a loss; keeping too much in cash after a downturn.

Damage: disposition effect; portfolios too conservative to meet goals.

Fix: focus on total-return and goals; reframe losses as useful (tax-loss harvesting); fewer statement checks.

Don't confuse: regret aversion is about the feeling of a wrong decision, not the loss itself.

cards.prompt: Define it, give an example, the damage it does, and how to overcome it
cards.back_html:
Overestimating one's knowledge, skill, or forecasting precision. Emotional

Example: trading daily and holding five stocks because "I know this sector."

Damage: excessive trading costs and taxes, under-diversification, underestimating risk.

Fix: keep a record of predictions vs outcomes; trading limits; a passive core with a small "satellite" for active ideas.

cards.prompt: Define it, give an example, the damage it does, and how to overcome it
cards.back_html:
Preferring to leave things as they are; inertia, even when a change would help. Emotional

Example: never changing a 401(k) allocation set at hire ten years ago.

Damage: the portfolio drifts away from the client's goals and risk level.

Fix: scheduled reviews; automatic rebalancing; defaults designed to be good (target-date funds).

Don't confuse: endowment is valuing something because you own it; status quo is general inertia.

cards.prompt: Define it, give an example, the damage it does, and how to overcome it
cards.back_html:
Valuing an asset more simply because you own it; you'd demand more to sell it than you'd pay to buy it. Emotional

Example: keeping inherited bank stock that is 40% of net worth "because Dad picked it."

Damage: concentration risk; refusal to rebalance.

Fix: "If you had this in cash, would you buy this stock?"; sell gradually; keep a small sentimental position.

cards.prompt: Define it, give an example, the damage it does, and how to overcome it
cards.back_html:
Avoiding decisions that might later cause regret, either by doing nothing or by following the crowd. Emotional

Examples: staying in cash after a crash ("if I buy and it drops again I'll feel terrible"); herding into popular stocks so you won't be alone if wrong.

Damage: missed returns, or herd risk at bubble prices.

Fix: decide rules in advance; diversify; dollar cost average into the market.

cards.front: Differentiating behavioral biases and how to overcome them
cards.prompt: Explain it as you would on a short-answer question
cards.back_html:
Cognitive biases come from faulty reasoning or memory: conservatism, confirmation, representativeness, mental accounting, anchoring, framing, recency. Moderate them with education, data, and checklists.

Emotional biases come from feelings: loss aversion, overconfidence, status quo, endowment, regret aversion. Harder to correct, so advisers often adapt the portfolio to them within reason.

Common look-alike pairs:

  • Conservatism (slow updating) vs confirmation (filtering).
  • Representativeness (stereotypes) vs recency (latest events).
  • Status quo (inertia) vs endowment (ownership).
  • Loss aversion (the loss) vs regret aversion (the wrong decision).
  • Anchoring (a number) vs framing (the wording).

General fixes: a written IPS, automation (auto-invest, rebalancing), diversification, and an adviser as a behavioral coach.

cards.prompt: Define it, give an example, and explain why it matters
cards.back_html:
Federal insurance on bank deposits: $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, per ownership category. Created by the Banking Act of 1933; backed by the full faith and credit of the U.S.

  • Covered: checking, savings, money market deposit accounts, CDs, cashier's checks.
  • Not covered: stocks, bonds, mutual funds (including money market mutual funds), ETFs, annuities, insurance, crypto, safe-deposit box contents.
  • Ownership categories stack: single, joint ($250k per co-owner), retirement (IRAs), trust, business.

Example: couple at one bank: her single $250k + his single $250k + joint $500k = $1M insured.

Contrast: SIPC covers brokerage customers up to $500k ($250k cash) if the firm fails, not market losses. NCUA covers credit unions at $250k.

cards.prompt: Formula, meaning, and a worked example
cards.back_html:
Net worth = total assets − total liabilities

A snapshot of wealth on one date, from the personal balance sheet. Assets are listed at fair market value.

  • Assets: cash/liquid, invested (brokerage, retirement), use/personal (home, cars).
  • Liabilities: current (credit cards, bills) and long-term (mortgage, auto, student loans).

Example: $650k assets − $410k liabilities = $240k net worth.

Tracking it over time shows whether the household is building wealth.

cards.prompt: Define it, give an example, and explain why it matters
cards.back_html:
Net cash flow (surplus or deficit) = cash inflows − cash outflows

Income and spending over a period (month or year), unlike the balance sheet's single date.

  • Inflows: salary, bonuses, interest, dividends, rent received.
  • Outflows: fixed (mortgage, insurance, loan payments), variable (food, travel), taxes.
  • A surplus funds saving and investing; a persistent deficit erodes net worth.
  • Records actual cash: a car bought with a loan shows only the payments.

cards.prompt: Formula, meaning, and a worked example
cards.back_html:
Savings ratio = amount saved ÷ income

The share of income the household saves. Textbooks use either gross or after-tax income as the denominator; state which you use.

Example: saves $1,200/month on $8,000 gross → 15% (on $6,000 take-home → 20%).

Common target: 10–15%+ of gross; Bernstein urges at least 15%. A low ratio signals the client can't fund long-term goals.

cards.prompt: Formula, meaning, and a worked example
cards.back_html:
DTI = total monthly debt payments ÷ gross monthly income

Measures debt burden and capacity to take on more; lenders use it to approve loans.

Example: mortgage $2,200 + car $450 + student loan $350 = $3,000 on $10,000 gross → 30%.

  • Front-end (housing only) guideline ≤ 28%; back-end (all debt) ≤ 36%; many mortgages allow up to 43%.
  • Lower is better: more room to absorb shocks.

cards.prompt: Formula, meaning, and a worked example
cards.back_html:
Split after-tax income: 50% needs, 30% wants, 20% savings and extra debt payoff (Elizabeth Warren, All Your Worth). The study guide calls it "50-20-30."

  • Needs: housing, utilities, groceries, insurance, transportation, minimum debt payments.
  • Wants: dining out, travel, entertainment, subscriptions.
  • Savings: emergency fund, retirement, investing, payments above minimums.

Example: $6,000 take-home → needs $3,000, wants $1,800, savings $1,200.

Applying it: if needs exceed 50%, cut housing/transport or trim wants. Limits: 50% is tight in high-cost areas; 20% may be too low for late starters.

cards.prompt: Formula, meaning, and a worked example
cards.back_html:
Year-1 withdrawal = 4% × portfolio; then raise that dollar amount by inflation each year
Nest egg needed = annual spending from portfolio ÷ 0.04 = 25 × spending

Bengen (1994) / Trinity Study: historically survived every 30-year U.S. period with ~50–75% stocks.

Example: needs $80k/year, Social Security covers $30k → $50k ÷ 0.04 = $1.25M. Year 2 at 3% inflation: $51,500.

  • Why useful: simple savings target, quick sustainability test, easy client conversation.
  • Limits: U.S. history only; 30-year horizon; ignores fees and taxes; rigid; vulnerable to sequence-of-returns risk.

cards.front: Ability vs willingness to take risk
cards.prompt: Explain it as you would on a short-answer question
cards.back_html:
Ability (capacity) is objective and financial: time horizon, wealth relative to needs, income stability, liquidity needs, flexibility of spending.

Willingness (tolerance) is subjective and psychological: attitudes, questionnaire answers, past behavior in downturns.

When they conflict, use the lower one. If willingness exceeds ability, ability is a hard limit. If ability exceeds willingness, educate, but respect the lower willingness; a client who panics and sells does more damage.

Example: young surgeon, secure income, 35-year horizon (high ability) who lost sleep in the last drop (low willingness) → average-to-below-average overall.

State the overall verdict as below-average, average, or above-average risk tolerance.

cards.prompt: Explain it as you would on a short-answer question
cards.back_html:
Higher expected return requires accepting higher risk. Investors are paid only for systematic risk, because unsystematic risk can be diversified away for free.

CAPM: E(Ri) = Rf + βi [E(Rm) − Rf]

Example: Rf 3%, market 9%, β 1.2 → 3 + 1.2 × 6 = 10.2%

  • Ladder: cash < short bonds < long bonds < large-cap stocks < small-cap / emerging-market stocks.
  • The extra return over Rf is the risk premium.

cards.front: Recommending an equity investment approach from an IPS
cards.prompt: Explain it as you would on a short-answer question
cards.back_html:
Match the client's IPS to approach and vehicle:

  • Fee-sensitive, believes markets efficient, OK with market returns → passive (index funds/ETFs).
  • Taxable, high bracket → ETFs/index funds; an SMA with tax-loss harvesting for larger accounts.
  • Wants a little outperformance with tight tracking → enhanced index (semi-active).
  • Return target above market, tolerates tracking error → active, or core-satellite.
  • Large account, wants customization / ESG / legacy positions → separately managed account.
  • Short horizon or high liquidity needs → less equity; large-cap, liquid holdings.
  • Long horizon, high ability and willingness → more equity, including small-cap and international.

Justify each recommendation by citing the specific IPS line it answers.

cards.prompt: Formula, meaning, and a worked example
cards.back_html:
E(Rp) = Σ wi × E(Ri)

A weighted average of the assets' expected returns.

Example: 60% stocks at 9%, 30% bonds at 4%, 10% cash at 2% → 5.4 + 1.2 + 0.2 = 6.8%

With scenarios, first find each asset's E(R) = Σ probability × return. Boom 30% × 20%, normal 50% × 8%, bust 20% × −10% → 6 + 4 − 2 = 8%.

Risk is not a weighted average (unless ρ = +1): σp² = w₁²σ₁² + w₂²σ₂² + 2w₁w₂ρσ₁σ₂.

cards.prompt: Explain it as you would on a short-answer question
cards.back_html:
The IPS sets objectives (return, risk) and constraints (time horizon, taxes, liquidity, legal, unique circumstances). Memory aid: RR TTLLU.

  • It guides asset allocation, manager selection, rebalancing, and reviews.
  • Evaluating: look for mismatches: a 9% return target with below-average risk tolerance; aggressive equity with a big near-term liquidity need; no tax discussion for a high-bracket client.
  • Constructing: state the required return, the overall risk verdict, then each constraint in a sentence, then the resulting allocation.

cards.prompt: Formula, meaning, and a worked example
cards.back_html:
The return the portfolio must (required) and would like to (desired) earn. State nominal vs real and net of fees.

Required return ≈ spending ÷ investable assets + inflation + fees

Example: $2M portfolio, $90k spending, 2.5% inflation → 4.5% + 2.5% = 7.0% (exact: 1.045 × 1.025 − 1 = 7.11%).

Then test it against risk tolerance. If the required return needs more risk than the client can bear, the client must spend less, save more, or work longer.

cards.prompt: Explain it as you would on a short-answer question
cards.back_html:
Combine ability (financial capacity) and willingness (psychology) into one verdict: below-average, average, or above-average. When they conflict, use the lower one.

  • Raises ability: long horizon, large assets relative to spending, stable income, few near-term needs, insurance in place.
  • Lowers ability: retirement soon, high withdrawal rate, concentrated assets, dependents, unstable income.
  • Willingness clues: questionnaire answers, words like "can't afford to lose," behavior in past crashes.

Example language: "Above-average ability, below-average willingness → average overall risk tolerance."

cards.prompt: Explain it as you would on a short-answer question
cards.back_html:
Cash the client needs from the portfolio on short notice or for known near-term expenses.

  • Ongoing spending needs (e.g., 1–2 years of withdrawals for a retiree).
  • Emergency reserve (3–6 months of expenses).
  • Planned outflows: home down payment, tuition, a new roof.

Example language: "$40k home down payment in 18 months plus a 6-month reserve; hold in cash or short-term bonds."

High liquidity needs reduce ability to take risk and favor liquid, large-cap holdings over illiquid assets.

cards.prompt: Explain it as you would on a short-answer question
cards.back_html:
How long until the money is needed. It can be single-stage or multi-stage.

  • Longer horizon → more ability to take risk (time to recover from losses).
  • Multi-stage example: "12 years to retirement, then ~30 years in retirement."
  • Stage changes (retirement, college start) trigger an IPS review.

Example: a 35-year-old saving for retirement has a long horizon; the same person saving for a house in 2 years has a short one for that goal.

cards.prompt: Define it, give an example, and explain why it matters
cards.back_html:
A gain on an asset held more than one year.

  • Taxed at preferential rates (0%, 15%, 20%), plus the 3.8% net investment income tax for high earners.
  • Waiting past one year can cut the tax sharply.

Example: $2,980 gain held 13 months at 15% → $447 tax (vs $953.60 at a 32% short-term rate).

cards.prompt: Define it, give an example, and explain why it matters
cards.back_html:
A gain on an asset held one year or less. Taxed at ordinary income rates.

Example: $2,980 gain held 6 months at a 32% bracket → $953.60.

High-turnover trading and active mutual funds generate more short-term gains, which is one reason they are tax-inefficient.

cards.prompt: Define it, give an example, and explain why it matters
cards.back_html:
Reduces taxable income. It saves tax equal to the deduction × your marginal rate.

Example: a $1,000 deduction in the 24% bracket saves $240.

  • Above-the-line (adjustments: traditional IRA, HSA, student loan interest) reduce AGI.
  • Below-the-line: the standard deduction or itemized deductions (mortgage interest, state/local taxes, charity), whichever is larger.
  • Worth more to higher-bracket taxpayers.

cards.prompt: Define it, give an example, and explain why it matters
cards.back_html:
Reduces tax owed dollar for dollar.

Example: a $1,000 credit saves $1,000, regardless of bracket.

  • Refundable credits can produce a refund below zero tax; nonrefundable credits stop at zero.
  • A $500 credit beats a $2,000 deduction for anyone below a 25% bracket (2,000 × 0.24 = $480).

cards.prompt: Define it, give an example, and explain why it matters
cards.back_html:
A distribution of a corporation's after-tax profits to its shareholders (owners).

  • Qualified: taxed at long-term capital gain rates. Requires a U.S. or qualified foreign corporation and holding the stock more than 60 days in the 121-day window around the ex-dividend date.
  • Ordinary (non-qualified): taxed at ordinary rates (REITs, money market funds, short holdings).
  • Not guaranteed; the board can cut it.
  • "Double taxation": profits are taxed at the corporate level, then again to the shareholder.

cards.prompt: Define it, give an example, and explain why it matters
cards.back_html:
Payment to a lender for the use of money: bonds, CDs, savings accounts.

  • Taxed as ordinary income.
  • Exceptions: municipal bond interest is federal-tax-exempt (often state too if in-state); Treasury interest is state-tax-exempt.
  • A legal obligation of the borrower, unlike dividends.
  • Deductible for the paying corporation, so it is taxed only once.

cards.prompt: Define it, give an example, and explain why it matters
cards.back_html:
Tax-loss harvesting: sell investments with losses to realize them and offset realized gains (and up to $3,000 of ordinary income per year). Reinvest in something similar so market exposure stays.

Wash-sale rule: buying a "substantially identical" security within 30 days before or after the sale disallows the loss (it's added to the new basis). Swap, e.g., one S&P 500 fund for a total-market fund.

Tax-gain harvesting: in years you fall in the 0% LTCG bracket, sell winners and rebuy to reset basis higher at no tax cost (no wash-sale rule for gains).

cards.prompt: Define it, give an example, and explain why it matters
cards.back_html:
• Hold more than one year for long-term rates.
  • Harvest losses; avoid wash sales.
  • Specific lot identification: sell highest-basis lots first (instead of FIFO).
  • Asset location: bonds, REITs, high-turnover funds in tax-deferred accounts; index funds/ETFs in taxable; highest growth in Roth.
  • Use tax-efficient vehicles: index funds, ETFs (in-kind redemptions).
  • Don't buy a mutual fund just before its capital gain distribution.
  • Donate appreciated shares to charity; hold to death for a step-up in basis.
  • Harvest gains in 0% years; use munis in high brackets; max out 401(k)/IRA/HSA.

cards.front: Calculating taxes on investments and property
cards.prompt: Formula, meaning, and a worked example
cards.back_html:
Gain = amount realized (sale price − selling costs) − adjusted basis

Basis = cost + commissions. For property, adjusted basis = cost + improvements − depreciation.

Stock: buy 100 sh at $50 + $10 commission (basis $5,010); sell at $80 − $10 ($7,990). Gain $2,980; long-term at 15% = $447.

Home: buy $400k + $50k improvements; sell $800k − $40k costs → gain $310k. Primary residence exclusion ($250k single / $500k joint, lived there 2 of last 5 years) → $0 recognized for a couple.

Rental: depreciation taken is recaptured (up to 25%). Inherited assets get a step-up in basis; gifts keep the giver's carryover basis.

cards.front: Capital gain vs capital loss (netting rules)
cards.prompt: Explain it as you would on a short-answer question
cards.back_html:
Gain = sold for more than adjusted basis; loss = sold for less.

  1. Net short-term gains vs short-term losses.
  2. Net long-term gains vs long-term losses.
  3. Net the two results against each other.
  4. A net loss offsets up to $3,000 of ordinary income per year ($1,500 married filing separately).
  5. The rest carries forward indefinitely, keeping its character.

Example: ST +8k −3k = +5k; LT +2k −12k = −10k → net −5k: deduct 3k, carry forward 2k (long-term).

Losses on personal-use property (your car, your home) are not deductible.

cards.prompt: Explain it as you would on a short-answer question
cards.back_html:
• Unrealized (paper) gain: the asset rose but hasn't been sold. Not taxed.
  • Realized gain: a sale or exchange occurred. Realized gain = amount realized − adjusted basis.
  • Recognized gain: the part of the realized gain reported as taxable this year.

Realized but not recognized: home-sale exclusion, 1031 like-kind real estate exchange (deferred), trades inside an IRA/401(k), gifts of stock to charity.

Example: $310k realized gain on a home; $500k exclusion → $0 recognized.

cards.prompt: Explain it as you would on a short-answer question
cards.back_html:
Earned: wages, salary, tips, bonuses, self-employment income. Subject to income tax and payroll tax (FICA 7.65%; self-employment 15.3%). Required to contribute to an IRA.

Unearned: interest, dividends, capital gains, rents, royalties, pensions, Social Security. No payroll tax; may face the 3.8% net investment income tax (above $200k single / $250k joint).

Kiddie tax: a child's unearned income above a threshold is taxed at the parents' rate.

cards.front: How dividends are taxed, and how they differ from interest
cards.prompt: Explain it as you would on a short-answer question
cards.back_html:
• Interest = return to a lender; deductible for the payer; taxed to you at ordinary rates.
  • Dividend = share of profits to an owner; paid from after-tax corporate income (double taxed); qualified dividends get LTCG rates (0/15/20%), ordinary dividends get ordinary rates.
  • Interest is a contractual obligation; dividends are discretionary.
  • Bondholders are paid before shareholders in bankruptcy.

Example: $1,000 of qualified dividends at 15% → $150 tax; $1,000 of bond interest at a 32% bracket → $320.

cards.front: After-tax yield and tax-equivalent yield (why relevant)
cards.prompt: Formula, meaning, and a worked example
cards.back_html:
After-tax yield = r × (1 − t)  ·  TEY = muni ÷ (1 − t)

Lets you compare taxable and tax-exempt bonds on what the investor actually keeps.

Example: 35% federal + 5% state ≈ 40%. Corporate 6% → 3.60%. Treasury 5% → 5 × 0.65 = 3.25%. In-state muni 4% → 4.00% (best); TEY = 4 ÷ 0.60 = 6.67%.

Munis make sense mainly for high-bracket investors. Break-even bracket = 1 − (muni ÷ taxable).

cards.front: Income tax flow, brackets, marginal vs effective rate (Piper)
cards.prompt: Formula, meaning, and a worked example
cards.back_html:
Gross income − adjustments = AGI
AGI − (standard or itemized deduction) = taxable income
Tax − credits − withholding = refund or balance due
  • Progressive brackets: each rate applies only to income inside that bracket; a raise never lowers take-home pay.
  • Marginal rate = rate on the next dollar (use for decisions). Effective rate = total tax ÷ income.

Example (made-up brackets): 10% to $20k, 12% to $80k, 22% above. Taxable $100k → 2,000 + 7,200 + 4,400 = $13,600; marginal 22%, effective 13.6%.

cards.prompt: Formula, meaning, and a worked example
cards.back_html:
Weighti = price × shares outstanding (often float-adjusted) ÷ total market cap

Bigger companies carry more weight. Examples: S&P 500, Nasdaq Composite, Russell indexes.

Example: A $100→$110 (1M sh), B $50→$45 (4M), C $30→$36 (10M). Total cap $600M → $650M = +8.33%.

  • Pros: reflects the market; self-rebalancing; low turnover; cheap to track.
  • Cons: overweights the largest (possibly overvalued) stocks; momentum and concentration risk.

cards.prompt: Formula, meaning, and a worked example
cards.back_html:
Index = sum of share prices ÷ divisor

Higher-priced stocks dominate, regardless of company size. Examples: Dow Jones Industrial Average, Nikkei 225.

Example: prices 100, 50, 30 → 60. After: 110, 45, 36 → 63.67 = +6.11%. A 10% move in the $100 stock moves it 5.6%; in the $30 stock, only 1.7%.

  • A stock split forces a divisor adjustment.
  • Weights are arbitrary, since share price says nothing about value.

cards.prompt: Formula, meaning, and a worked example
cards.back_html:
Every stock gets the same weight; index return = simple average of the stock returns. Example: S&P 500 Equal Weight.

Example: returns +10%, −10%, +20% → +6.67%.

  • Pros: diversified by name; tilts toward smaller (and often value) stocks.
  • Cons: must rebalance often (turnover, costs, taxes); gives small, illiquid stocks big weights.

cards.prompt: Formula, meaning, and a worked example
cards.back_html:
HPR = (P1 − P0 + D) ÷ P0

Total return (price change + income) over the whole time you held the investment, any length.

Example: buy $40, $1 dividend, sell $46 → (6 + 1) ÷ 40 = 17.5%

Annualize a multi-year HPR: (1 + HPR)1/years − 1. A 3-year HPR of 33.1% = 10%/year.

cards.prompt: Formula, meaning, and a worked example
cards.back_html:
G = [(1 + r1)(1 + r2)…(1 + rn)]1/n − 1

The compound annual growth rate actually earned.

Example: +50% then −50%: arithmetic = 0%, geometric = (1.5 × 0.5)½ − 1 = −13.4%. $100 really became $75.

  • Geometric ≤ arithmetic; the gap grows with volatility (G ≈ A − σ²/2).
  • Use geometric for past compound performance; arithmetic for a single future year's expected return.

cards.prompt: Formula, meaning, and a worked example
cards.back_html:
Σ CFt ÷ (1 + IRR)t = 0

The discount rate that makes the present value of all cash flows (outflows negative, inflows positive) equal zero. In portfolio measurement, IRR is the money-weighted return.

Without Excel: two periods → set x = 1/(1 + r) and solve the quadratic. Otherwise, guess rates (10%, 12%, 14%) until NPV ≈ 0, or use a financial calculator's CF/IRR keys.

Example: −100 now, −120 at t1, +260 at t2 → 260x² − 120x − 100 = 0 → x = 0.8925 → IRR = 12.05%.

The study guide lists IRR twice; it's one concept.

cards.prompt: Explain it as you would on a short-answer question
cards.back_html:
The IRR of the investor's actual cash flows. It reflects the investor's experience, including the timing and size of deposits and withdrawals.

Example: buy 1 share at $100; at $120 buy another; sell both at $130 ($260). MWR = 12.05% vs TWR 14.02%: more money was in for the weaker second year.

  • Use when the manager controls cash flows (private equity) or to show a client's real result.
  • Unfair for judging a manager who doesn't control flows.

cards.prompt: Formula, meaning, and a worked example
cards.back_html:
TWR = [(1 + r1)(1 + r2)…(1 + rn)]1/n − 1, breaking periods at each cash flow

Removes the effect of external contributions and withdrawals, so it measures the manager's skill. Required by GIPS; the industry standard.

Example: year 1: 100 → 120 = 20%; year 2: 120 → 130 = 8.33%. TWR = (1.20 × 1.0833)½ − 1 = 14.02%.

cards.prompt: Formula, meaning, and a worked example
cards.back_html:
Real = (1 + nominal) ÷ (1 + inflation) − 1

Return in terms of purchasing power. Retirement and IPS goals should be judged in real terms.

Example: geometric return 5.05% with 3% inflation → 1.0505 ÷ 1.03 − 1 = 1.99% real.

Nominal returns can look healthy while real returns are near zero (e.g., the 1970s). Bernstein calls inflation the most likely "deep risk."

cards.prompt: Formula, meaning, and a worked example
cards.back_html:
E(R) = Σ ps × Rs  ·  or CAPM: Rf + β(Rm − Rf)

The probability-weighted average of possible outcomes; a forward-looking estimate, not a promise.

Example: 30% × 20% + 50% × 8% + 20% × (−10%) = 6 + 4 − 2 = 8%.

For a portfolio: weighted average of the holdings' expected returns.

cards.prompt: Define it, give an example, and explain why it matters
cards.back_html:
Market-wide risk that affects nearly all securities: interest rates, inflation, recessions, war, policy shocks. Also called market or non-diversifiable risk.

  • Measured by beta.
  • Rewarded with higher expected return (CAPM), because it can't be diversified away.
  • Can be reduced only by holding less equity (or hedging), not by adding more stocks.

cards.prompt: Define it, give an example, and explain why it matters
cards.back_html:
Company- or industry-specific risk: lawsuits, a CEO departure, product recall, fraud, a failed drug trial. Also called specific, idiosyncratic, or diversifiable risk.

  • Largely eliminated with ~20–30 stocks across industries.
  • Not rewarded: investors can remove it for free.
  • Total risk (variance) = systematic + unsystematic. The unsystematic share ≈ 1 − R².

cards.prompt: Formula, meaning, and a worked example
cards.back_html:
σ = √[ Σ (Rt − R̄)² ÷ (n − 1) ] (sample)  ·  σ = √[ Σ ps(Rs − E[R])² ] (scenarios)

How widely returns spread around their mean: a measure of total risk. If returns are normal, ~68% fall within ±1σ, ~95% within ±2σ.

Example: 10%, −5%, 15% → mean 6.67%; squared deviations 11.11 + 136.11 + 69.44 = 216.67; ÷ 2 = 108.33 → σ = 10.41% (population ÷3: 8.50%).

cards.prompt: Formula, meaning, and a worked example
cards.back_html:
Cov(A,B) = Σ ps (RA,s − E[RA]) (RB,s − E[RB])

Measures whether two assets' returns move together.

  • Positive: tend to move the same way. Negative: opposite ways. Near zero: unrelated.
  • Its size is hard to interpret (unbounded, depends on units), so we standardize it into correlation.
  • Drives the cross term in portfolio variance: 2w₁w₂Cov₁₂.

cards.prompt: Formula, meaning, and a worked example
cards.back_html:
ρAB = Cov(A,B) ÷ (σA × σB)

Standardized covariance, from −1 to +1.

  • +1: no diversification benefit. 0: unrelated. −1: perfect hedge.
  • Any ρ < 1 makes portfolio risk lower than the weighted average of the risks.

Example: Cov 0.0096, σA 20%, σB 12% → 0.0096 ÷ 0.024 = 0.40.

Correlations tend to rise in crises, when diversification is most needed.

cards.prompt: Formula, meaning, and a worked example
cards.back_html:
βi = Cov(Ri, Rm) ÷ σm² = ρi,m × σi ÷ σm

Sensitivity to market moves; the measure of systematic risk.

Example: ρ 0.8, σi 25%, σm 16% → 0.8 × 25/16 = 1.25. Moves ~1.25% per 1% market move.

  • Market β = 1; T-bills β = 0; β < 1 defensive; β > 1 aggressive.
  • Portfolio beta = weighted average of the holdings' betas.

cards.prompt: Define it, give an example, and explain why it matters
cards.back_html:
R² = ρ² with the benchmark: the share of a fund's return variation explained by the benchmark.

Example: ρ = 0.8 → R² = 0.64 (64% explained by the market).

  • High R² (≳ 0.85): beta and alpha are meaningful. Very high R² plus high fees can flag a closet indexer.
  • Low R²: wrong benchmark or a very different strategy; beta and alpha are unreliable.
  • A falling R² vs the stated benchmark can reveal style drift.

cards.prompt: Formula, meaning, and a worked example
cards.back_html:
IR = (Rp − Rb) ÷ tracking error, where tracking error = σ(Rp − Rb)

Active return per unit of active risk: the best gauge of an active manager's skill and consistency vs the benchmark.

Example: fund 11%, benchmark 9.5%, tracking error 3% → 1.5 ÷ 3 = 0.50.

~0.5 is good; 1.0 is exceptional. Enhanced-index strategies historically post the highest IRs.

cards.prompt: Explain it as you would on a short-answer question
cards.back_html:
(Rp − Rf) ÷ β

Reward per unit of systematic risk. Use it for a fund that is one slice of a diversified portfolio.

Compare: Fund A 11%, β 0.9 → 8.89%. Fund B 9%, β 1.1 → 5.45% (Rf 3%). A wins on Treynor.

If A loses on Sharpe but wins on Treynor, A carries lots of unsystematic risk: fine inside a diversified portfolio, poor as a client's only holding.

cards.prompt: Explain it as you would on a short-answer question
cards.back_html:
(Rp − Rf) ÷ σ

Reward per unit of total risk. Use it for a client's entire portfolio or a stand-alone holding.

Compare: Fund A 11%, σ 18% → 0.44. Fund B 9%, σ 12% → 0.50. B wins on Sharpe.

  • Which measure: whole portfolio → Sharpe; diversified slice → Treynor; downside focus → Sortino; active skill → information ratio; beat CAPM? → alpha.

cards.prompt: Formula, meaning, and a worked example
cards.back_html:
Jensen's α = Rp − [Rf + βp(Rm − Rf)]

Return above (or below) what the portfolio's beta says it should have earned under CAPM. Positive alpha = value added by the manager.

Example: Rp 12%, Rf 3%, β 1.2, Rm 10% → required 3 + 8.4 = 11.4% → α = +0.6%.

Simpler "active return" = Rp − benchmark return. Alpha is only meaningful when R² is high.

cards.front: Active vs passive vs semi-active (enhanced index) strategies
cards.prompt: Explain it as you would on a short-answer question
cards.back_html:
Active return = Rp − Rbenchmark; tracking risk = σ of active return.

  • Passive: match the index. Active return ~0, tracking risk near 0, lowest fees and taxes. Rationale: markets are largely efficient; costs are certain, alpha isn't.
  • Semi-active / enhanced index: small controlled tilts. Active return ~0.5–2%, tracking risk ~0.5–2%. Historically the highest information ratios.
  • Active: aims to beat the index meaningfully. Higher active return target, tracking risk often 4%+, highest fees and turnover. Rationale: skill can exploit mispricing.

Sharpe's arithmetic: before costs, the average active dollar earns the market return; after costs, it must trail passive. Core-satellite blends a passive core with active satellites.

cards.prompt: Explain it as you would on a short-answer question
cards.back_html:
What: invest a fixed dollar amount on a fixed schedule regardless of price.

How: average cost = total $ ÷ total shares; it's always ≤ the average price because more shares are bought when prices are low.

When to use: paycheck investing (401(k) contributions are natural DCA); a nervous investor with a windfall who would otherwise stay in cash; volatile markets.

Caution: with a lump sum in hand, investing it all at once has beaten DCA about two-thirds of the time historically, because markets rise more often than they fall. DCA's real value is behavioral (reduces regret).

cards.prompt: Explain it as you would on a short-answer question
cards.back_html:
A professional manages a portfolio of individual securities owned directly by the investor.

  • Pros: customization (exclude stocks, ESG screens, work around legacy positions); lot-level tax-loss harvesting; no embedded gains from other investors; full transparency.
  • Cons: high minimums (~$100k–$250k+); fees ~0.5–1.5%+; more paperwork and statements; harder to diversify in small accounts.
  • Best for: large, taxable, high-bracket clients who want control.

cards.prompt: Explain it as you would on a short-answer question
cards.back_html:
Pooled investment vehicle; investors own fund shares, priced once a day at NAV.

  • Pros: low minimums, professional management, instant diversification, easy automatic investing.
  • Cons: higher expense ratios, possible loads and 12b-1 fees; capital gain distributions (you can be taxed on gains from others' redemptions and manager turnover); cash drag; style drift; no customization; end-of-day pricing only.

cards.prompt: Explain it as you would on a short-answer question
cards.back_html:
Mutual funds (or ETFs) that track an index passively.

  • Pros: very low cost (~0.03–0.2%); low turnover → tax-efficient; broad diversification; no manager risk or style drift.
  • Cons: can't beat the index (earn the market minus small costs); must hold overvalued stocks in a cap-weighted index; index fund versions still trade once a day and can distribute some gains.
  • Bernstein's and Bogle's recommended core holding.

cards.prompt: Explain it as you would on a short-answer question
cards.back_html:
Pooled funds that trade on an exchange throughout the day like stocks.

  • Pros: very low expense ratios; most tax-efficient (in-kind creation/redemption avoids distributing gains); no minimums beyond one share; intraday trading, limit orders, shorting, options; transparent holdings.
  • Cons: bid-ask spreads and possible commissions; can trade at a premium/discount to NAV; temptation to overtrade; risky niche, leveraged, and inverse ETFs.

cards.front: Investment style: small, mid, large cap
cards.prompt: Explain it as you would on a short-answer question
cards.back_html:
Rough cutoffs: small ~$300M–$2B, mid ~$2–10B, large > $10B market cap.

  • Rationale: small-cap premium (Fama-French size factor); less analyst coverage → more mispricing; large caps offer stability and liquidity.
  • Risks: small caps are more volatile, less liquid, more likely to fail.
  • Manager difficulties: capacity limits as assets grow; winners "graduate" out of the style and must be sold; higher trading costs; index providers set different size breakpoints.

cards.prompt: Explain it as you would on a short-answer question
cards.back_html:
Value: low P/E, P/B, high dividend yield. Rationale: markets overreact; prices mean-revert; value premium. Risk: value traps (cheap because the business is declining).

Growth: high earnings growth, high P/E. Rationale: earnings growth drives prices. Risk: overpaying; sharp drops on earnings disappointments.

Blend / GARP (growth at a reasonable price) sits between.

Manager difficulties: styles go in and out of favor for years (value lagged through the 2010s), creating pressure to drift; definitions differ by index provider; stocks migrate between styles.

cards.prompt: Explain it as you would on a short-answer question
cards.back_html:
• Rationale for international: diversification (correlation < 1); access to faster-growing economies; currency diversification; counters home bias.
  • Risks: currency risk; political and regulatory risk; less liquidity; different accounting standards; emerging-market data quality.
  • Manager difficulties: higher trading and custody costs; foreign withholding taxes (foreign tax credit helps in taxable accounts); correlations rise in global crises, just when diversification matters.

cards.prompt: Explain it as you would on a short-answer question
cards.back_html:
Past performance is a weak predictor of future results; few top-quartile funds stay on top (SPIVA persistence studies).

  • Use risk-adjusted measures (information ratio, Sharpe, alpha), net of fees.
  • Compare against the right benchmark and peer group.
  • Look over a full market cycle, with the same manager in charge.
  • Watch for survivorship bias and cherry-picked periods.
  • Pair it with qualitative due diligence: people, philosophy, process, firm stability.

cards.prompt: Explain it as you would on a short-answer question
cards.back_html:
Fees are the most reliable predictor of future relative performance: low-cost funds tend to beat high-cost peers.

  • Fees are certain; alpha is not. A manager must beat the index by more than the fee just to break even.
  • Fees compound: 1% a year on $100k over 30 years at 7% costs ~$176k vs a 0.05% fund.
  • Check total cost: expense ratio, loads, 12b-1, advisory/wrap fees, trading costs from turnover.
  • Very high R² + active fees = closet indexer: paying active fees for index returns.

cards.prompt: Explain it as you would on a short-answer question
cards.back_html:
A manager strays from the stated style (a small-cap value fund buying large-cap tech growth).

  • Why it matters: distorts the client's planned allocation; creates hidden overlap with other managers; makes the benchmark and performance evaluation meaningless.
  • Causes: chasing performance when the style is out of favor; asset growth pushing into larger stocks.
  • Detect it: holdings-based analysis, returns-based style analysis, falling R² vs the stated benchmark.

cards.front: External cash flows: effect on time-weighted vs money-weighted returns
cards.prompt: Explain it as you would on a short-answer question
cards.back_html:
• TWR is unaffected by contributions and withdrawals (periods are broken at each flow and linked).
  • MWR is affected: money added before strong periods pushes MWR above TWR; money added before weak periods (or withdrawn before strong ones) pushes it below.

Example: $1,000 falls to $800; client adds $1,000; next year +25% → $2,250. TWR = 0.0%; MWR = 8.11% (bought the dip).

Judge a manager on TWR (they don't control flows). MWR shows the client's actual experience; the gap is the "behavior gap."

cards.front: Data quality issues with returns (lying with statistics)
cards.prompt: Explain it as you would on a short-answer question
cards.back_html:
• Survivorship bias: dead funds drop out, inflating averages.
  • Backfill / instant-history bias: funds join databases after good records.
  • Incubation bias: only winning test funds are launched publicly.
  • Cherry-picked periods (end-point sensitivity).
  • Wrong benchmark, or a price index vs a total-return fund.
  • Arithmetic instead of geometric averages.
  • Gross of fees and taxes instead of net.
  • Annualizing short periods; cumulative shown as annual.
  • Backtested or hypothetical results (look-ahead bias).
  • Stale pricing of illiquid assets, which smooths volatility.
  • Returns quoted without risk.

cards.front: Evaluating the quality of a benchmark
cards.prompt: Explain it as you would on a short-answer question
cards.back_html:
A valid benchmark is SAMURAI:

  • Specified in advance
  • Appropriate to the manager's style
  • Measurable
  • Unambiguous (known holdings and weights)
  • Reflective of the manager's current opinions
  • Accountable (manager accepts it)
  • Investable (could be held passively)

Red flags: chosen after the fact; style mismatch (S&P 500 for a small-cap fund); low R² between fund and benchmark; a price index used against a dividend-collecting fund.

cards.front: Hurdles an active manager faces in beating an index
cards.prompt: Explain it as you would on a short-answer question
cards.back_html:
• Costs: management fees, commissions, bid-ask spreads, market impact, cash drag, taxes from turnover.
  • Zero-sum game before costs, negative-sum after (Sharpe's arithmetic).
  • Competition and efficiency: professionals trade against professionals; information spreads instantly.
  • Size: success attracts assets; big funds can't trade small stocks without moving prices.
  • Career risk and herding: managers hug the benchmark (closet indexing).
  • Evidence: SPIVA reports roughly 85–90% of U.S. large-cap funds trail the S&P 500 over 15 years (approximate).

cards.prompt: Explain it as you would on a short-answer question
cards.back_html:
• Market: execute now at best available price. Certain execution, uncertain price.
  • Limit: buy at or below / sell at or above a set price. Certain price, may not fill.
  • Stop (stop-loss): becomes a market order when the stop price hits; can fill far below in a gap.
  • Stop-limit: becomes a limit order at the stop; may not fill.
  • Trailing stop: stop price follows the market up.
  • Short sale: borrow, sell, buy back later; profits if price falls; unlimited loss potential; pay dividends to lender; margin required.
  • Margin purchase: borrow to buy (Reg T 50% initial; ≥25% maintenance). Call price = P₀(1 − IM) ÷ (1 − MM): $50 × 0.5 ÷ 0.7 = $35.71.
  • Time-in-force: day, GTC, fill-or-kill, immediate-or-cancel, all-or-none.

cards.front: How fees and commissions affect returns (calculation)
cards.prompt: Formula, meaning, and a worked example
cards.back_html:
FV ≈ PV × (1 + r − fee)n

Fee drag: $100k, 7% gross, 30 years → 0.05% fee ≈ $751k; 1% fee ≈ $574k. The 1% fee costs ~$176k.

Front load: $10,000 at 5.75% → $575 fee, $9,425 invested. Offer price = NAV ÷ (1 − load) = $20 ÷ 0.9425 = $21.22. Needs +6.1% to break even.

Commissions: buy 200 at $50 + $25; sell at $55 − $25 → gain $950 on $10,025 = 9.48% vs 10% gross.

Fee types: expense ratio, front/back/level loads (A/B/C shares), 12b-1, advisory (AUM ~1%), wrap, spreads, performance fees ("2 and 20").

cards.front: Key factors that influence a stock's price
cards.prompt: Explain it as you would on a short-answer question
cards.back_html:
• Earnings and growth, especially vs expectations (surprises).
  • Interest rates: higher rates raise the discount rate and lower values.
  • Inflation and the business cycle.
  • Dividends and buybacks.
  • Valuation multiples and sentiment: fear, greed, momentum, biases.
  • Industry, competition, management quality.
  • Supply/demand and liquidity: fund flows, index inclusion.
  • Policy and events: Fed, taxes, regulation, geopolitics, currency.
Gordon growth: P₀ = D₁ ÷ (r − g)

$2 ÷ (8% − 4%) = $50; if r rises to 9% → $40 (−20%).

cards.prompt: Explain it as you would on a short-answer question
cards.back_html:
Plain-English guide to U.S. income tax; its sample problems are fair game on the exam.

  • Flow: gross income → AGI → taxable income → tax → credits → refund or balance due.
  • Deduction vs credit; above- vs below-the-line; standard vs itemized.
  • Marginal vs effective rate; progressive brackets.
  • Filing status.
  • Short- vs long-term gains, netting, $3,000 loss limit, carryforwards.
  • Qualified vs ordinary dividends; interest as ordinary income.
  • FICA and self-employment tax.
  • Traditional vs Roth: traditional if your rate now is higher than in retirement; Roth if lower.

cards.front: Bill Bernstein (If You Can / Four Pillars / Deep Risk)
cards.prompt: Explain it as you would on a short-answer question
cards.back_html:
• Save at least 15%, starting young.
  • Simple three-fund portfolio: U.S. total stock, international stock, U.S. bonds, in low-cost index funds; rebalance periodically.
  • Four pillars: theory (risk and return are inseparable; diversify), history (bubbles and crashes recur), psychology (you are your own worst enemy), business (the industry profits from your fees and mistakes).
  • You can't reliably time markets or pick winning managers.
  • Shallow vs deep risk: shallow = temporary drop; deep = permanent loss of real wealth (inflation, deflation, confiscation, devastation). Stocks are the best long-run inflation defense.

Check which Bernstein title was assigned.
